_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for São Tomé and Príncipe covering uninhabited discovery, Portuguese sugar plantations, slave trade, cocoa 'islands of chocolate', roça plantation system, forros and angolares communities, independence 1975, democratic transition, and contemporary challenges.

ethnic_groups.name: Mestiço (Forros/Filhos da Terra)
ethnic_groups.notes: Mixed African-Portuguese; descended from freed slaves and settlers; dominant social group; Forro Creole language

ethnic_groups.name: Angolares
ethnic_groups.notes: Descended from escaped Angolan slaves (maroons); southeastern São Tomé; distinct Angolar Creole; fishing communities

ethnic_groups.name: Servicais (Contract Workers)
ethnic_groups.notes: Descendants of contract labourers from Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde brought for cocoa roças; often Cape Verdean origin

ethnic_groups.name: Tongas
ethnic_groups.notes: Children of servicais born on islands; intermediary social position

ethnic_groups.name: Principense
ethnic_groups.notes: Native to Príncipe island; Lung'ie Creole speakers; distinct from São Tomean culture

ethnic_groups.name: European (Portuguese)
ethnic_groups.notes: Small Portuguese community; returnees and expatriates

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Nigerian, Gabonese, and other African communities

country_profile.notes_unique: Second-smallest African country by area and population; no indigenous population; entirely settled by Portuguese colonists and African slaves from 1470s

prime_minister.name: Patrice Trovoada
prime_minister.notes: ADI; son of first PM Miguel Trovoada; previously PM 2008–2010 and 2014–2018

former_presidents.name: Manuel Pinto da Costa
former_presidents.notes: Founding president; MLSTP; Marxist-Leninist era; returned via election 2011 as independent

former_presidents.name: Miguel Trovoada
former_presidents.notes: First democratically elected; ADI; survived 1995 and 2003 coup attempts

former_presidents.name: Fradique de Menezes
former_presidents.notes: Businessman; survived 2003 coup; presided over oil exploration deals

910.name: Volcanic Formation and Uninhabited Islands
910.description: São Tomé and Príncipe form as volcanic islands on the Cameroon Line; unlike most African territories, the islands were uninhabited before Portuguese arrival.

sub_clusters.name: Geological Origins and Cameroon Line
sub_clusters.description: Volcanic islands formed along the Cameroon Line hotspot chain; Pico de São Tomé (2,024m) and Pico do Príncipe; unique biodiversity evolves in isolation.

sub_clusters.name: Pre-Discovery Ecology and Endemism
sub_clusters.description: Islands develop extraordinary endemic species: giant sunbird, São Tomé ibis, and unique plant species; no human settlement before 1470.

920.name: Portuguese Discovery and First Settlement
920.description: Portuguese navigators discover the islands c.1470–1471; initial colonisation with degredados (exiled convicts), Jewish children, and enslaved Africans.

sub_clusters.name: Discovery and Initial Colonisation
sub_clusters.description: João de Santarém and Pêro Escobar reach São Tomé (c.1470) and Príncipe (1471); first settlers include Portuguese degredados and Jewish children exiled from Portugal.

sub_clusters.name: Early Sugar Plantation Economy
sub_clusters.description: Álvaro de Caminha establishes sugar plantations using enslaved African labour; São Tomé becomes the world's largest sugar producer by the 1520s; model later exported to Brazil.

930.name: Sugar Economy and Atlantic Slave Trade Hub
930.description: São Tomé serves as a critical entrepôt in the Atlantic slave trade; sugar production declines as Brazilian competition rises; mixed-race forro community emerges.

sub_clusters.name: Slave Trade Entrepôt
sub_clusters.description: São Tomé becomes a major staging post for the Atlantic slave trade between West Africa and the Americas; tens of thousands pass through annually.

sub_clusters.name: Slave Revolts and Angolares
sub_clusters.description: Major slave revolt led by Amador 1595; escaped slaves (angolares) establish independent maroon communities in the island interior; Amador briefly captures the capital.

sub_clusters.name: Emergence of Forro Society
sub_clusters.description: Mixed-race forro ('free') population emerges from unions between Portuguese settlers and enslaved African women; forros become local landed elite; distinct Creole culture and language develop.

940.name: Cocoa Economy and Roça Plantation System
940.description: Cocoa replaces sugar; São Tomé becomes the world's largest cocoa producer by 1908; the roça plantation system uses contract labourers (serviçais) in conditions of virtual slavery.

sub_clusters.name: Cocoa Revolution and 'Islands of Chocolate'
sub_clusters.description: Cocoa introduced early 19th century; massive expansion under Portuguese planters; São Tomé becomes world's largest cocoa producer by 1908; known as 'the chocolate islands'.

sub_clusters.name: Roça System and Cadbury Boycott
sub_clusters.description: Roça (plantation) system uses contract labourers (serviçais) from Angola, Mozambique, and Cape Verde in conditions of virtual slavery; Cadbury chocolate boycott 1909 draws international attention.

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Decline and Batepá Massacre
sub_clusters.description: Cocoa prices decline; planters demand more forced labour; Batepá massacre of February 1953 kills hundreds of forro workers protesting forced labour; galvanises independence movement.

950.name: Independence Movement and MLSTP
950.description: The MLSTP (Movimento de Libertação de São Tomé e Príncipe) leads the independence struggle from exile; Carnation Revolution in Portugal enables independence.

sub_clusters.name: MLSTP Formation and Exile Struggle
sub_clusters.description: Manuel Pinto da Costa and others found the MLSTP in exile (Libreville, then Accra); linked to other Portuguese African liberation movements; limited guerrilla capacity.

sub_clusters.name: Independence (12 July 1975)
sub_clusters.description: Portuguese Carnation Revolution April 1974 ends dictatorship; negotiations lead to independence 12 July 1975; Manuel Pinto da Costa becomes first president; MLSTP single-party socialist state.

950.name: Socialist Single-Party Period
950.description: MLSTP single-party socialist state; nationalisation of roças; economic decline; dependence on Soviet bloc and Angola; forced democratic opening.

sub_clusters.name: Nationalisation and Economic Decline
sub_clusters.description: Plantations nationalised; Portuguese managers flee; cocoa production collapses; food shortages; dependence on foreign aid.

sub_clusters.name: Mercenary Invasion Attempt (1978)
sub_clusters.description: Alleged mercenary plot to overthrow government; Angolan troops stationed as deterrent; heightened security and political repression.

960.name: Democratic Transition
960.description: São Tomé becomes one of Africa's first multiparty democracies; Miguel Trovoada elected 1991; political instability but democratic norms generally hold.

sub_clusters.name: Multiparty Democracy Established
sub_clusters.description: 1990 referendum approves multiparty constitution; Miguel Trovoada wins 1991 election; first peaceful transfer of power in lusophone Africa; Fradique de Menezes elected 2001.

sub_clusters.name: 2003 Mini-Coup
sub_clusters.description: Military officers briefly seize power while President Menezes is abroad; international mediation by Nigeria; democratic rule restored within a week.

960.name: Contemporary São Tomé and Príncipe
960.description: Oil exploration raises hopes and corruption risks; democratic consolidation; tourism potential; climate vulnerability of small island state.

sub_clusters.name: Oil Exploration and Economic Hopes
sub_clusters.description: Joint Development Zone with Nigeria; oil exploration raises expectations of wealth; corruption concerns; actual production remains minimal.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Consolidation and Fragile Economy
sub_clusters.description: Regular democratic elections; coalition politics; heavy aid dependence; cocoa still dominant export; ecotourism development; vulnerability to climate change and sea-level rise.

sub_clusters.name: Roça Heritage and Cultural Identity
sub_clusters.description: Abandoned roça plantations become cultural heritage sites; forro, angolar, and tonga communities maintain distinct identities; Creole languages and cultural revival.
